doc_summary: Ryan Greenblatt surveys AI control measures across software infrastructure, AI/human components, and security, emphasizing adversarial evaluation with highly realistic synthetic inputs and limiting what AIs can infer about their situation. The post stresses procedural, threat-model-driven methodology over fixed lists of measures.

items.claim: In a setup, do generate maximally realistic synthetic inputs (ideally indistinguishable from real ones by a trained discriminator) instead of ad hoc fake scenarios because the AI should not be able to tell a lucky break from an adversarial input.
items.quote: We'd likely want to have a general purpose synthetic data generation process which generates very realistic possible inputs to AIs. Ideally, our pipeline would be so good that AIs can't be trained to discriminate between real (normal) inputs and fake (normal) inputs generated by this pipeline.

items.claim: In a setup, build fake inputs by modifying real inputs (or censoring real ones) instead of writing them from scratch because this makes fabricated inputs more realistic and easier to produce.
items.quote: There are a variety of tricks to make fake inputs more realistic, such as constructing them by modifying real inputs. We could also censor information from (actual) inputs so that faking inputs is easier.

items.claim: In a setup, make the test scenario realistic but rare/abnormal (e.g. bad actions atypically easy) instead of testing on typical inputs because it prevents the model from directly testing whether it can discriminate the red-team inputs from real ones.
items.quote: Note that we probably want to mostly use our pipeline to generate realistic, but abnormal/rare inputs (e.g. inputs where doing some bad action is atypically easy) so it is less easy to directly test whether the AI can discriminate the actual inputs we use for redteaming.

items.claim: Prefers removing distribution shifts and hard-to-fake aspects of inputs (information-preserving transformations) over trying to generate perfectly realistic fakes because the transformed input distribution may be much easier to simulate.
items.quote: One perspective on this is that it might be hard to generate realistic looking fake inputs, but might be much less difficult to find some information preserving transformation such that the resulting distribution of inputs is actually reasonably easy to generate.

items.claim: In a setup, withhold scaffolding-level cues (current time, whether control measures changed, pause status, KV-cache side channels) instead of leaving them visible because models can pick up subtle signals about being tested or rerun.
items.quote: Ideally, AIs would only know what they need to know, and thus the scaffolding and other infrastructure wouldn't inform them about things like the current time, whether control measures have been updated, what other jobs are running, whether they had been paused, etc.

items.claim: Test for subtle side channels that let a model infer it is being paused, rerun, or in a different inference setup, rather than assuming it can't tell.
items.quote: Minimally, we should test for this sort of side channel so that we can have some understanding of whether AIs know if they were paused or if they are now being run with slightly different inference code.

items.claim: Prefers fake-evidence tests (e.g. presenting fabricated evidence of being caught) evaluated adversarially because models should only react to very hard-to-fake evidence, which makes the model's response to the scenario informative.
items.quote: We should of course adversarially evaluate whether AIs strike if they are presented with (fake) evidence that they've been caught to force AIs to only escalate like this in response to very hard to fake evidence

items.claim: Use infrastructure to cheaply and indistinguishably simulate environment responses to the AI's actions, replacing with a smarter process where simulation fails, because some environment parts need intelligence to fake convincingly.
items.quote: Some parts of the environment will require intelligence to simulate in a way that is indistinguishable to the AI, but having infrastructure for simulating where possible and replacing with a more intelligent process when simulation isn't possible still seems helpful.

items.claim: Distrusts non-online/offline training and test distributions that are off the distribution of interest because scheming AIs may distinguish training or test from real deployment.
items.quote: Non-online training has the disadvantage of not being exactly on the distribution of interest (potentially yielding suboptimal performance) and also potentially allowing scheming AIs to distinguish between when they are in training vs not.

items.claim: Prefers a procedural approach of adversarial threat analysis plus control evaluations and testbeds over implementing a fixed list of measures because the right measures should be determined empirically against what AIs could cause.
items.quote: rather than approaching control from the perspective of "we should implement XYZ measures", I think it would generally be more effective to establish a process for determining what methods are worthwhile both via testbed/benchmark driven development and via abstract threat modeling and analysis.

items.claim: Is skeptical that anomaly-detection on treacherous turns can be validated without real in-the-wild examples, so offline evidence for it is weak.
items.quote: it isn't at all clear whether this would work and I don't see how we'd gain much confidence in this technique prior to seeing multiple treacherous turns in the wild.
